# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXVIII. A FAST DAY

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Prior to the start of classes the following morning, a extraordinary meeting was held by the Good-Conduct Club. Once several ideas had been put forward, the members agreed that enduring a fast day would serve as a suitable penalty.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0000 }

“For an entire day, not one thing will pass our lips,” Tobias declared. “Besides, I have a bit of curiosity about how fasting feels. We can discover it now through this opportunity.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0001 }

“Which day are we going to pick for this?” inquired Ida, who believed it was going to be an entirely simple penalty and felt somewhat surprised that Tobias and Grace had failed to invent a more difficult one.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0002 }

“Monday would be a good choice,” Grace suggested. “Our Sunday evening meals are usually rather heavy, and what we eat on Mondays is never very substantial anyway.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0003 }

“But that’s just the point,” Tobias cried out. “We ought not to fast on the easiest day, but on the most difficult—and Sunday fits that description, since, as you mentioned, our meal that day is usually roast beef rather than cold ditto. Going without ditto would hardly be a punishment. Let us choose next Sunday. That day will work well, because father plans to trade morning service duties with the minister from Upper Kettlebridge. Father won't return until evening. Should Aunt Martha question our behavior, we will state plainly to her that our fasting is for our souls' benefit, pointing out that it appears in the Bible and telling her to leave us alone, which I expect she will.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0004 }

Aunt Martha failed to do so. She simply remarked in her irritable, muttered manner, “What foolishness are you young rips up to now?” and promptly dismissed it from her mind. Prior to anyone rising, Mr. Ashdown had departed early that morning. Furthermore, he left without eating his morning meal, though such an event was naturally a frequent happening. He omitted it half the time, and no person existed to bring it to his attention. Missing breakfast—the breakfast prepared by Aunt Martha—did not constitute a severe ordeal. Abstaining from the “lumpy porridge and blue milk” that had provoked the disdain of Mary Stubbs was not considered any major loss, even by the famished “young rips.” Nevertheless, the situation altered when dinner time arrived. Their hunger was ravenous by then, and the scent of roast beef that filled the manse—a scent entirely delicious, even though the meat was severely undercooked—proved nearly unbearable to them. Out of sheer despair, they hurried to the graveyard to escape the aroma. However, Ida was unable to avert her gaze from the dining room window, which revealed the Upper Kettlebridge minister calmly consuming his food.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0005 }

“If I were merely able to obtain a tiny, little portion,” she uttered with a sigh.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0006 }

“Now, cease doing that,” Tobias ordered. “It is obviously difficult—however, that constitutes the penalty. Right now, I am hungry enough to consume an idol, yet do you hear me grumbling? We should focus on a different topic. Superiority over our appetites is what we must achieve.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0007 }

When the hour for supper arrived, the intense pangs of hunger that had plagued them during the earlier part of the day were no longer felt by them.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0008 }

“It seems to me that we are becoming accustomed to the situation,” Grace remarked. “A remarkably strange, completely hollow sensation comes over me, yet I am unable to claim that I feel hunger.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0009 }

“My mind feels strange,” Ida stated. “At times, it spins and spins.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0010 }

Yet she attended church courageously alongside the rest. Had Mr. Ashdown not been so completely absorbed in and captivated by his topic, he perhaps would have observed the pallid small face and sunken eyes sitting in the manse pew below. However, he observed nothing at all, and the sermon he delivered went on somewhat longer than was typical. Subsequently, right before he announced the last hymn, Ida Ashdown fell from the manse pew's seat and remained unconscious on the floor.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0011 }

The initial person to get to her was Mrs. Elder Clow. Taking the slender small frame out of the pale, frightened arms of Grace, she bore it inside the vestry. Mr. Ashdown, neglecting the hymn along with all other matters, hurried wildly behind her. By whatever means they managed, the congregation dispersed on its own.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0012 }

“Oh, Mrs. Clow,” Grace gasped, “has Ida died? Is she dead because of us?”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0013 }

“What is wrong with my child?” the pallid father inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0014 }

“I believe she has merely lost consciousness,” Mrs. Clow stated. “Oh, thank goodness, the doctor is here now.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0015 }

Reviving Ida proved to be quite a difficult task for Hugh. A considerable period elapsed while he tended to her before she unclosed her eyes. After that, he transported her to the manse, with Grace trailing behind, weeping uncontrollably out of relief.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0016 }

“You see, she is merely hungry—she failed to eat any food today—no one among us did—all of us were fasting.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0017 }

“Fasting!” exclaimed Mr. Ashdown, and “Fasting?” queried the doctor.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0018 }

“Indeed—as a penalty on ourselves because we sang Polly Wolly inside the graveyard,” Grace remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0019 }

“Do not make yourselves suffer for that, my child,” Mr. Ashdown said, upset. “You received your small reprimand from me—and every one of you showed remorse—and you were forgiven by me.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0020 }

“Yes, but punishment was necessary for us,” Grace clarified. “In our Good-Conduct Club—you know—it’s our rule that whenever we do something wrong, or something that might harm father in the congregation, self-punishment is required. We are raising ourselves, you know, since there isn’t anyone else to do it.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0021 }

A groan escaped Mr. Ashdown, yet the doctor, carrying a look of relief, rose from beside Ida.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0022 }

“Therefore, this young girl merely collapsed because she lacked nourishment, meaning a hearty dish is all that she requires,” he stated. “Mrs. Clow, would you have the goodness to ensure she receives one? Furthermore, judging by what Grace told us, I believe every one of them could use a bite of food, lest additional people pass out.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0023 }

“I guess making Ida fast was a mistake,” Grace stated with regret. “Thinking about it, punishment should have fallen solely on Tobias and me. We organized the concert, plus we were the eldest.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0024 }

“The same as everyone else, I sang Polly Wolly,” Ida’s faint, small voice uttered, “which meant I needed to receive punishment, as well.”
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0025 }

Mrs. Clow arrived bearing a glass of milk, Grace along with Tobias and Rupert crept away to the pantry, and John Ashdown retired to his study, sitting in the dark for an extended period, solitary with his bitter reflections. Thus, his offspring were raising themselves owing to the fact that there was “nobody to do it”—laboring through their small confusions absent a guiding hand or a counseling voice. The phrase innocently spoken by Grace festered within her father’s thoughts like a barbed arrow. There was “nobody” to attend to them—to give solace to their little souls and tend to their small bodies. How delicate Ida had appeared, resting on the vestry sofa during that prolonged swoon! How slender were her tiny hands, how pale her small face! It seemed as though she could drift away from him in a single breath—sweet little Ida, whom Cecilia had pleaded with him to guard so carefully. Ever since his wife died, he had not experienced such a painful terror as when he had leaned over his small daughter during her state of unconsciousness. Action was required of him—yet what action? Ought he to request Elizabeth Kirk to be his wife? A good woman was she—she would show kindness to his offspring. He might force himself to take that step were it not for the affection he felt for Clementine Ainslie. However, until he had stamped that feeling out, he was unable to approach a different woman with a proposal of marriage. And stamping it out proved impossible—his attempts had failed. Clementine had attended church that very evening, marking her first appearance since coming back from Portmaris. A glimpse of her countenance at the rear of the packed sanctuary had met his eyes, precisely as he concluded his sermon. A wild pulse had surged in his heart. With bowed head and vibrant veins, he remained seated while the choir performed the “collection piece.” He had not laid eyes on her since the night he had requested her hand in marriage. On standing up to announce the hymn, his hands had been shaking and a flush had covered his pale face. Subsequently, Ida’s loss of consciousness had driven every thought from his memory for a while. At present, surrounded by the dark and isolation of the study, it returned forcefully. Clementine stood as the sole woman in existence for him. Attempting to wed any other was pointless for him. Even on behalf of his offspring, he could not perpetrate such a desecration. His load had to be carried by him alone—an effort had to be made to become a superior, more attentive father—his children had to be instructed not to fear approaching him regarding all their minor difficulties. Afterwards, he lit his lamp and picked up a thick recently published volume that was causing great controversy in the theological sphere. A single chapter would be read by him to quiet his thoughts. A mere five minutes afterward, he had become oblivious to the world and its attendant worries.
{: #nw-v05-c28-p0026 }
